# Essay Prompts

## Prompt 1: Repository Setup and Shared Ownership

> Explain how your group created its CEP repository from the MSDM CEP template, selected an appropriate visibility setting, invited collaborators, and ensured that every member cloned the same repository. Clearly distinguish among using a template, creating a repository, and cloning a repository.

Group 9 created our CEP repository by first reviewing all assigned videos, correcting the hyperlink to access the repository containing the CEP template (there is an extra parenthesis that takes the viewer to a 404 error). After locating the CEP template folder, we then clicked `Use this template`, followed by `Create a new repository`. This new folder uses the template instructed to duplicate all project files without editing the original repository.

We chose a URL that clearly outlines our group number, the project, our client, and our faculty lead: `GP9CEP-RKR.Kwok` accompanied by a more clearly defined description. After inviting all members, Dr. Jung and Dr. Kwok were also invited to our publicly accessible repository. All immediate team members confirmed accessibility and cloned our collective folder to their local drives.

> Why would independently cloning or copying the original template create problems for group collaboration?

Independently cloning or copying the original template would mean multiple project files and documents, effectively excluding the member who is not working from the cloned files from contributing.

**Principle Author: Leeann Lewis-Waddell**

## Prompt 2: Local, Remote, and Working Files

> Explain the relationship among the files on your computer, the local Git repository, and the remote repository on GitHub. In your explanation, distinguish among saving, staging, committing, pushing, fetching, and pulling.

The remote repository is the point of origin for all group members' contributions, from which all updates must first be pulled to update the local Git repository in order to work from the most up-to-date version of the project stored locally on each member's drive.

To update the project locally, members must first fetch and then pull data from the GitHub repository. Once local files are up to date, members will make changes and then save them locally, which must then be staged in the local GitHub, before committing with a message to describe the changes. After changes are committed, they must be pushed and synced to update the remote repository.

> Why does saving a QMD file on your computer not make the change available to your teammates?

Simply saving a QMD file on your computer does not make changes available to team members because the save is local. Changes must be staged, committed, then pushed before group members can pull updates.

**Principal Author: Leeann Lewis-Waddell**

Our group completed Round 1 using a sequential workflow so that each member worked from the most recent version of the shared report. After one person finished their assigned section, they rendered the document, committed their changes, and pushed them to GitHub. The next member then pulled the updated version before beginning their own work. This helped make sure that everyone was working from the same version of the QMD file instead of separate or outdated copies.

The sequential process also helped reduce the chance of merge conflicts. Since group members were not all editing the same report at the same time, Git was less likely to encounter competing changes to the same lines. It also created a clearer commit history because each person's contribution could be connected to a specific section and commit message.

## Prompt 4: A Reliable Everyday CEP Workflow

> Create a numbered checklist that a group member should follow every time they work on the CEP report, beginning before they edit and ending after they push. Explain why pulling before editing and using focused, descriptive commits make collaboration safer and make the project's history more useful.

For Group 9, a reliable workflow begins with communication. Since we are contributing to the same QMD file, we should follow these steps each time we work on the CEP report: 1. Check the group chat to confirm the assigned section and make sure it is your turn to edit. 2. Open the Col-Practice project in RStudio or Positron and confirm that you are working in the correct repository and on the main branch. 3. Review the Git status to make sure there are no unfinished local changes. 4. Pull the latest version from GitHub before making any edits. 5. Review the newest changes so that you understand what the previous group member added. 6. Add or revise only the section assigned to you. 7. Save the QMD file and render the report to verify that the HTML file is created without errors. 8. Review the rendered report and the Git diff to make sure the content and formatting appear as intended. 9. Stage only the files related to your work and create a commit with a clear description of what you completed. 10. Push the commit to GitHub, confirm that it appears in the repository, and notify the group that the next person can begin.

Pulling before editing is important because it ensures that each Group 9 member begins with the most recent version of the report. If someone starts working from an older local copy, that person may unknowingly overwrite another member's work or create a merge conflict. Following a sequential process allows us to work in either RStudio or Positron while still maintaining one shared and current version of the report. Clear and focused commit messages also make the project history easier to understand. For example, Add Carmen's responses for prompts 4 and 9 explains both the author and the purpose of the change, while a message such as update provides very little useful information. Descriptive commits will help our group and instructor follow the order of contributions, identify who completed each section, and locate or reverse a specific change if a problem appears later.

**Principal author: Carmen Lia Jimenez**

## Prompt 5: Coordinating Work and Preventing Merge Conflicts

> Explain what may happen when two people edit the same lines of the same QMD file and then attempt to push their work. Describe at least three practices your group will use during the CEP to reduce merge conflicts. Include how your group will divide sections, communicate who is editing, and decide when work is ready for another member.

When two people edit the same lines on the QMD file, GitHub might not be able to automatically combine and make the changes. If one person were to push their work first, the second person might get a merge conflict when they try to push or pull. Git will mark the conflicting section in the popup box and our group would have to choose which version we want to keep or how to combine each version before pushing it.

3 practices that we will use during CEP:

1.  We will divide the QMD file into sections and assign a section to each person. We can split these sections to reduce more than one person working on one section at the same time. This will also push us to keep constant communication and will also help us stay on track of our tasks

<!-- -->

2.  We currently have discord where we communicate, so we will continue to use this tool to communicate when we are editing a file. Like I said in the last practice, communication is key so talking to each other and letting each other know when we are working on a section will prevent another person from editing the same lines.

<!-- -->

3.  Our group will pull the most recent version of the GitHub repo regularly either in RStudio or Positron before starting new work. We also have to make sure to push and commit our changes. The commit description is very important because it lets us communicate what changes we have made.

Overall, we have to have clear communication and have a scheduled plan and workflow that allows us to stay organized to reduce any merge conflicts throughut the CEP.

## Prompt 6: Responding to a Push Rejection or Merge Conflict

> Consider this situation: A group member edits the report without pulling first. Meanwhile, another member pushes changes to the same section. Git rejects the first member's push, and a merge conflict appears after pulling.
>
> Explain, in order, what the first member should do. Describe how the member would use Positron's Merge Editor or the conflict markers in the file to compare the current and incoming changes, decide what content to retain, remove the conflict markers, render and inspect the report, commit the resolution, and push it. Also explain why force-pushing, deleting a teammate's work, or replacing the repository with an older local copy would be inappropriate.

The first member should pull the most recent changes from the GitHub after their push is rejected. Because two members edited the same section, Git might create a merge conflict.

The next step would be for the first member to open the conflicted QMD file, in this situation it would be Positron. Then they can use the Merge Editor or look at the conflict markers in the file to compare their changes with the incoming changes from the other group member. Then the members will decide which parts they want to keep. It depends on the situation, but sometimes it is better to just keep one version, but there may be situations where they would need to combine both versions.

Once they decide what they want to keep, the first member should remove the conflict markers and double check to make sure that the section is correctly written. Then they should save and render the QMD report to make sure there is no errors when they run it, and the report looks good to go.

Force-pushing, deleting a teammate’s work, or replacing the repo with an older local copy is inappropriate because it could erase any changes that were already added by other group members. On top of this, it is a group project, everyone’s name is on it and everyone is working hard on it, so it would be very disrespectful and cause unwanted drama within the group.

## Prompt 7: Branches, Issues, and Pull Requests

> Based on the collaboration video, explain the purposes of a GitHub Issue, a branch, and a pull request. How could these tools support task assignment, review, and approval during a longer CEP project? Contrast this approach with making a small, coordinated change directly on the main branch. Identify at least one situation in which your group should prefer a branch and pull request.

A GitHub Issue provides a place to describe a task, report a problem, or propose an improvement. Our group can use issues to assign responsibilities and keep related discussions together. A branch allows a member to develop changes separately from the main version of the report. A pull request proposes bringing those changes into another branch, such as `main`, and gives teammates a place to review the differences, ask questions, and request revisions before merging. During a longer CEP project, these tools can connect an assigned task to the work completed and the review that follows.

A small, coordinated change, such as correcting a typo in an assigned section, may be made directly on `main` when the group knows who is editing and the member follows the pull, edit, render, review, stage, commit, and push workflow. More substantial changes benefit from a branch and pull request because teammates can evaluate them before they become part of the main report. For example, our group should use a branch and pull request when revising the analysis methodology or reorganizing several report sections. These changes could affect other members’ work and should be reviewed for accuracy, consistency, and successful rendering before merging.

**Principal author: Georgia Monjarrez**

Since all of these changes are shown in the same repository, we can see that everyone contributed to the same shared project.

The commit history also makes it clear who worked on each part and what they changed. Each commit is connected to a specific person and has a message explaining what was added or updated. This makes it easier to follow how the report came together and who was responsible for each section.

One commit message that I thought was especially effective was `Add Carmen's responses for prompts 4 and 9 and repair RStudio project`. I think this was a good commit message because it clearly explains what Carmen added and also mentions the extra change she made to the project. Someone looking at the commit history can understand what she did without having to open the files first.

## Prompt 9: Security, Confidentiality, and Repository Hygiene

> Explain what materials must never be pushed to the CEP repository, even when it is private. Address confidential client data, personally identifiable information, passwords, API keys, access tokens, temporary files, and locally generated files that do not belong under version control. Explain the role of .gitignore, and discuss what a student should do before proceeding if they are uncertain whether a file may be shared.

Before adding any file to our CEP repository, we need to consider whether it is appropriate and safe to share. Confidential client materials, personally identifiable information, passwords, API keys, access tokens, authentication files, and information covered by an NDA should never be pushed to GitHub. Personally identifiable information may include names, email addresses, phone numbers, or individual survey responses that could be connected to a specific person. Group 9 should also avoid committing temporary or unnecessary files, such as .DS_Store, caches, logs, and raw datasets that have not been approved for sharing. Because our repository is currently public, we need to be especially careful about everything we stage and commit. However, changing a repository to private would not make it appropriate to store sensitive information, since access can still be granted accidentally and content may later be published through GitHub Pages.

The .gitignore file helps keep the repository organized by telling Git which files or file patterns should remain untracked. For example, it can exclude system files, temporary output, local environment files, and files containing credentials. However, .gitignore only helps prevent untracked files from being added; it does not remove a file that has already been committed or erase it from the repository's history. If a Group 9 member is unsure whether a file may be shared, that person should stop before staging or committing it. The group should review the client agreement and course requirements and, when necessary, ask the faculty lead, instructor, or authorized client contact for guidance. Until permission is confirmed, the file should remain outside the repository. When possible, our group should use approved, de-identified data and keep passwords or other secrets in secure environment variables instead of placing them directly in scripts or QMD files.

**Principal author: Carmen Lia Jimenez**

## Prompt 10: Group Collaboration Agreement

> Develop a short Git/GitHub collaboration agreement that your group will follow for the remainder of the CEP.

::: {.callout-note title="Group Collaboration Agreement"}
Our group agrees to follow these practices throughout the CEP:

1.  **Pull and push:** Every member will pull the latest changes before editing. After completing a contribution, they will save, render, review, stage, commit, and push their changes, then verify that the commit appears on GitHub.

2.  **Assign responsibilities:** We will divide work by task or report section and record each member’s responsibilities and deadlines in our group communication channel.

3.  **Coordinate editing:** During this practice assignment, we will edit the shared QMD file one person at a time. Members will announce when they begin editing and confirm when their changes have been pushed so the next person can begin. During the larger CEP, we will coordinate simultaneous work to avoid overlapping edits.

4.  **Use descriptive commits:** Each commit will contain a focused change and a message explaining what was completed, such as “Add collaboration agreement” or “Revise explanation of pull requests.”

5.  **Use branches and pull requests:** We will use branches and pull requests for substantial revisions or changes that need teammate review. Another member will review these changes before they are merged into main. Small, coordinated corrections may be made directly on main.

6.  **Handle conflicts together:** If a push is rejected because newer changes exist on GitHub, the member will pull or sync and review the result. For merge conflicts, the affected members will compare both versions, agree on the content to retain, remove conflict markers, render and inspect the report, and commit and push the resolution. We will not force-push or discard a teammate’s work to bypass a conflict.

7.  **Check rendering:** Each member will render and inspect the report after editing. The group will designate a final editor to pull all changes, render the complete report, verify formatting and links, and push the final QMD and HTML files before submission.

8.  **Protect confidential information:** We will exclude confidential client data, personally identifiable information, passwords, API keys, and access tokens from the repository. We will review files before staging and use .gitignore to exclude temporary and unnecessary local files. If we are unsure whether material may be shared, we will consult the instructor before including it.

All group members have reviewed this agreement and agree to follow it for the remainder of the CEP.
:::

**Principal author: Georgia Monjarrez**
